analysis.one_liner: Curbs brand-name drug patent tactics and speeds approval of cheaper generic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2000 with a bipartisan pair of cosponsors, sent to the Senate health committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies can keep cheaper generic copies off the market for years by listing extra patents on a drug, filing delay petitions with the FDA, and manipulating the rules that give the first generic maker a head start. This bill would narrow the patents a brand-name company can use to block generics, stop FDA review from being stalled by routine company petitions, allow more types of tests to prove a generic works the same, and move the generic to market sooner when the first challenger stalls. It never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and insurers who pay for prescription drugs, because generic versions typically cost far less than brand-name versions; the bill also helps generic drug makers get to market faster.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would limit the patents a brand-name company can use to block generic approval to patents on the drug's active ingredient or its first approved use, rather than the long list of secondary patents companies currently cite to delay competitors [S2][S3].

It would stop the FDA from delaying review of a generic application just because a company filed a citizen petition, unless the petition shows substantial scientific proof of a threat to public health and safety [S2][S3].
It would let a drug qualify as bioequivalent using broader tests, including comparative pharmacodynamic studies or in vitro methods, not only tests measuring absorption rate and extent [S2][S3].

It would speed the date a generic is approved when the first generic applicant fails to launch its drug, withdraws, or changes its patent certification after a settlement or loss in court, targeting the practice of paying the first generic challenger to stay off the market [S2][S3].
The bill states the sense of Congress that generic drugs should be made more available to reduce health care costs, echoing the purpose of the 1984 Hatch-Waxman Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose years of extra monopoly revenue from secondary patents, delay petitions, and settlements with generic challengers. Consumers could bear a small added safety-review risk if generics are approved on broader test methods.

drawbacks.text: The bill broadens the kinds of studies that can establish a generic is equivalent, including in vitro methods and limited confirmation studies; supporters of stricter testing worry some generics could be approved on less direct evidence of identical behavior in patients [S2][S3].

Narrowing the patents that can block generic approval could reduce brand-name companies' incentive to develop new formulations, combination products, and new uses of existing drugs, since those would no longer delay competition [S3].
The bill targets delay tactics but does not address other drivers of drug prices, and one of its provisions is only a nonbinding statement of congressional opinion [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: generic competition is the main mechanism by which drug prices fall, and the bill attacks three specific delay tactics at once. The main honest tradeoff is a modest risk that some generics are approved on thinner equivalence evidence, plus a plausible slowdown in minor product improvements. On balance the bill was a serious, narrowly targeted attempt to speed competition rather than a sweeping price control.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in September 2000, never got a hearing or markup, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Greater Access to Affordable Pharmaceuticals Act on September 14, 2000, joined by Sen. John McCain and Sen. Tim Johnson [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and bills not passed die with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the patent-listing, petition-delay, and settlement tactics the bill targeted, and consumers kept paying brand-name prices longer. Generic makers and patients did not get the faster pathway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept their delay tactics

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to curb brand-name patent tactics and speed generic approval.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor, making the effort bipartisan.

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry holding patents on approved drugs
against.what_they_did: Opposed Hatch-Waxman reform efforts of this era that would curtail patent-based delays of generic competition.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat joined by a prominent Republican and a second Democrat — but the bill never reached a vote, so how the full Senate would have split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would cut off their main tools for extending monopoly pricing after core patents lapse: listing secondary patents, citizen-petition delays, and settlements that keep the first generic off the market. Those tactics cost consumers billions in the form of years of brand-name prices [S2][S3].
Clearer patent rules, faster FDA review, and tougher first-generic exclusivity rules would get generics to market sooner, and their success is exactly what lowers drug costs for patients [S2][S3].
